title: Baca County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Baca County wells have a 270-foot median depth. Compare reported yields, water levels and estimated finished-well costs of $15,400-$26,800.
h1: Baca County well depths, water supply and drilling costs
intro_html:
Baca County’s well records lean heavily toward agricultural water, not household supply. Irrigation accounts for 54% of recorded uses, so the county’s high reported yields need context before you apply them to a home site.

Colorado DWR records include 5,376 permitted wells here, with 1,783 recorded as constructed. The 270-foot median depth is a useful budgeting reference, but a parcel near Springfield, Walsh or Campo needs a closer look at neighboring well logs, permitted use and current pumping performance.

sections.heading: A 270-foot starting point, not a depth guarantee
sections.html:
Among 3,198 wells reporting depth, Baca County’s median is 270 feet. The middle half runs from 175 to 392 feet. For a drilling bid, that means allowing for a substantial depth range rather than pricing every lot at the county median. The 90th-percentile depth is 496 feet; the deepest record, 4,249 feet, is not a sensible residential budget target.

Alluvium and plains sedimentary rock make the local water-bearing layers important. Permits name Southern High Plains and Ogallala aquifers, while many use an unnamed / fractured-bedrock category. That broad record label does not establish granite conditions on your parcel. Compare nearby completion logs for water-bearing intervals, casing and total depth before setting a target.

sections.heading: Why the 650 gpm median is not a household promise
sections.html:
The 915 records with pump yields report a median of 650.0 gpm and a middle half of 172.5–1000.0 gpm. Those figures belong to a countywide dataset where irrigation represents 54% of uses, stock 27% and domestic/household use 12%. They are not a forecast for a new domestic well.

Reported yields fall below 1 gpm in 1% of records, with another 1% in the 1–5 gpm band. Low-output wells exist even in this high-yield dataset. For a buyer, a low-yield result means investigating sustained output, recovery and possible storage needs before committing. A historical pump-yield entry is neither a current pumping test nor permission to withdraw that amount.

sections.heading: Recent Baca County water levels deserve a closer look
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to resting water, not the bottom of the well. Among 212 reporting records, the median is 134 feet below ground, and the middle half spans 43–195 feet. Pump selection also needs the water level under pumping, which a static measurement does not provide.

Decade medians were 76 feet in the 1950s, 90 in the 1960s, 64 in the 1970s, 80 in the 2010s and 180 in the 2020s. The recent readings suggest deeper water, but this is not a steady downward trend or a same-well monitoring series. Different wells and locations may affect the comparison. Request dated measurements and a current pumping test for the property itself.

sections.heading: An agricultural drilling history that continues today
sections.html:
Baca County’s permit history includes 955 permits issued in the 1960s and 782 in the 1970s. More recent records show 563 in the 2010s and 274 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The latest decade is incomplete, so its total should not be compared as though it covers the same period.

The most active drillers in these records are Ralph'S Welding (Woods, Ralph R), with 226 entries; Hegwood Drilling (Hegwood, Spencer), with 201; and Konkel Drilling (Konkel, David Leroy), with 132. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. Ask prospective drillers about recent work near your parcel and familiarity with its likely aquifer.

sections.heading: Budgeting a finished well near Springfield or Walsh
sections.html:
The Baca County cost model uses $35–$55 per foot for drilling through alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 270-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $9,400–$14,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $15,400–$26,800.

Use those figures as a planning range, not a parcel-specific quote. The 175–392-foot middle depth range leaves meaningful room for the drilling portion to change. Ask bidders to spell out casing, grout, well development, testing and pump equipment, along with how additional depth is charged. On a lot outside Springfield or Walsh, confirm the proposed well location and utility route before comparing finished-system prices.

sections.heading: Check water quality, low output and the septic layout
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 18 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 4 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. These entries are reasons to investigate location and testing history; they do not establish that a particular well is contaminated. A sampling site is not automatically a confirmed contamination source.

Have a qualified laboratory test the property’s water, including bacteria and nitrate, and discuss PFAS testing in light of nearby site information. Inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage. For new construction, coordinate the well, septic system, replacement area and building footprint before excavation. Even with strong county yield figures, address low-yield or unsuccessful drilling in the contract rather than assuming usable water is guaranteed.

sections.heading: Before buying a lot in Campo, Vilas or Two Buttes
sections.html:
Start with the actual parcel, not a countywide average. Around Campo, Vilas, Two Buttes or Pritchett, compare neighboring permits and completion logs for depth, aquifer, reported yield and measurement dates. Then match the seller’s well to its DWR permit and construction documents.

Confirm that the permitted use covers your plans. Do not assume a household well authorizes irrigation or every livestock use; exempt-well restrictions and augmentation requirements may affect what is possible. For an existing well, obtain current pumping and water-quality results. For an unbuilt lot, establish permit feasibility, drilling access, septic suitability and a written well budget before treating the land as ready to build.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Baca County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth in Baca County is 270 feet, based on 3,198 depth records. The middle half spans 175–392 feet, and the 90th percentile is 496 feet. Those figures help frame a drilling budget, but neighboring completion logs and the parcel’s water-bearing layers are better guides for an individual site.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Baca County?
faq.a: The local model estimates drilling at $35–$55 per foot. At the 270-foot median depth, the drilled hole costs about $9,400–$14,800, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $15,400–$26,800. Get a site-specific quote that identifies casing, grout, testing and charges for additional depth.

faq.q: How much water can a Baca County well produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 650.0 gpm median, but irrigation makes up 54% of recorded uses, so that is not a household-well expectation. Among reporting wells, 1% produce under 1 gpm and 1% fall in the 1–5 gpm band. Verify sustained output and recovery with a current pumping test, and check the permit’s authorized use.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Baca County?
faq.a: County records cannot establish the safety of an individual well. Mapped records within about 10 miles include 18 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 4 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites, but proximity alone does not prove contamination. Test the property’s water for bacteria and nitrate, discuss PFAS testing with a qualified laboratory, and inspect wellhead protection and nearby septic conditions.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Baca County?
faq.a: The decade medians suggest deeper water recently: reported static levels were 80 feet below ground in the 2010s and 180 feet in the 2020s. Earlier decades fluctuate, however, and these are not necessarily repeated measurements from the same wells. Treat the pattern as a reason to investigate, not proof of a specific property’s decline.
